name: Colored sunglasses lenses

lead: Colored sunglasses lenses are tinted eyewear chosen for style. A yellow, rose, orange or blue tint gives a distinct frame-and-colour look that shows straight away.

The tint changes how the wearer sees colour and contrast: yellow and orange filters reduce short-wavelength light, which a study linked to higher contrast, with some loss of colour discrimination. Research on tinted lenses covers vision and medical light sensitivity such as migraine and blepharospasm, not how attractive a face looks.

paras: People match tint colour and frame shape to their face and outfit, wearing them outdoors, at events or as a signature accessory.
Studies note reduced colour discrimination with some tints. The sources reviewed document no other harms.

web.title: Tinted Sunglasses: Does the Color Matter? - Revant Optics

angle.text: A tinted lens in yellow, rose, orange or blue gives a styled, put-together look the moment it goes on. Research on tints covers contrast and light sensitivity rather than appearance.

lead: Colored sunglasses lenses are tinted lenses, such as yellow, orange, rose, brown, gray or blue, worn for style and for the way each tint changes contrast and glare. A tint changes the color of the wearer's view and, depending on the color, can alter contrast and color discrimination.[1][2]

For looks, the lens color is part of the face's visual styling. Frames and tints frame the eye area, hide or soften it, and add a color accent, which is why tinted shades appear across fashion eyewear from aviators to wayfarers.[3] People who regard the eye area as a key feature use tints to change how that area reads in photos and in person. Sunglasses have been a fashion accessory since the 1930s and have been tied to film stars, musicians and subcultures.[3]

Published research on tinted lenses concerns vision and medical symptoms such as contrast, light sensitivity, migraine and blepharospasm, and has not examined how tint color changes perceived facial attractiveness.

paras: Sunglasses date back centuries in various forms. Wikipedia records Inuit snow goggles of flattened ivory, reports of smoky quartz lenses worn by Chinese judges, and Venetian tinted glasses in the 18th century, with mass production of inexpensive celluloid sunglasses beginning in 1929 and polarized lenses in 1936 [3]. Film stars helped spread them in the 1920s, and later styles such as aviators, wayfarers, teashades and wraparounds became tied to celebrities and subcultures [3].

Wikipedia describes tint effects: gray and green are regarded as neutral, brown increases contrast at the cost of some colour distortion, amber and yellow sharpen object definition in haze or snow, and yellow is not recommended for night driving [3]. It also states that lens darkness does not indicate UV protection and that experts recommend lenses blocking nearly all UVA and UVB up to 400 nm, often labelled UV400 [3].

The Aviator was designed by Bausch and Lomb in 1936 for US military pilots and was later worn by Douglas MacArthur and by 1970s musicians including Paul McCartney and Freddie Mercury; its popularity fell by 1980 and revived around 2000.[3] The Ray-Ban Wayfarer, introduced in 1952, was worn by James Dean, Elvis Presley and the Beatles and overtook Aviators in sales in 2012.[3] Round wire-rimmed teashades were associated with 1960s counterculture figures such as John Lennon and Mick Jagger, and oversized 1980s styles returned as a trend in the late 2000s.[3] Hunter S. Thompson wore yellow-tinted driving glasses.[3]

Wikipedia also records Crookes lenses (1913), designed to block ultraviolet light, and tinted spectacles in 18th-century Venice and 19th-century railway travel [3]. Alongside these, Wikipedia describes sunglasses as serving to hide the eyes or conceal visible conditions as well as to protect them [3].

Gray and green are regarded as neutral lenses that preserve true colors, brown increases contrast with some color distortion, turquoise enhances contrast without significant distortion, and yellow and amber improve object definition and are used for skiing and hunting, while blue or purple lenses help shooters see orange targets against green backgrounds.[3]

Photochromic lenses darken in UV light and lighten when it drops, although car windscreens filter UV and can stop them adjusting while driving. Mirrored lenses use a metallic, partly reflective coating that deflects light and whose color is independent of the tint beneath, and polarized lenses reduce glare from non-metallic surfaces such as water and roads.[3] Polarization, introduced in 1936 after Edwin Land's Polaroid filter, is generally considered unsuitable for pilots because of interference with some displays.[3]

Eyewear retailers describe lens color as a styling decision as well as an optical one. One manufacturer's guide characterises gray as the neutral, timeless option that keeps colors natural, green as a natural-looking tint used in ball sports, brown as softening light and aiding depth perception, yellow as softening blue light and pairing with warm skin tones, rose or pink as a vibrant choice that boosts contrast on snow, and blue as a bold style said to suit cool skin tones.[4] These pairings of tint with skin tone are style opinions from retailers rather than tested rules, and no published study has examined them.[4]

The wider tinted-lens revival is described in fashion and retail coverage as drawing on retro and early-2000s looks, with lighter translucent tints that leave the eyes visible and darker mirrored or opaque lenses that conceal them. For people who regard the eye area as a key feature, the choice runs between showing the eyes through a light tint and masking them with a dark one.[3][4]

Wikipedia lists ISO 12312 as the international standard for sunglasses, with the European Union rating lenses in categories 0 to 4 and the United States following ANSI Z80.3 [3]. Common lens materials are glass, polycarbonate and CR-39 plastic, and frames may be plastic, metal, nylon or wood [3].

Photochromic lenses rely on molecules that switch reversibly between a colourless and a coloured form when exposed to light; silver chloride and organic families such as naphthopyrans and spirooxazines have been used [5]. Wikipedia's photochromism entry notes that organic dyes switch more slowly inside a rigid lens and gradually lose performance through fatigue [5].
For driving, Wikipedia says fixed-tint lenses transmitting under 8 percent of light are unsuitable, and pilots are advised to avoid polarized lenses [3].

Wikipedia notes that prolonged UV exposure can cause photokeratitis, cataracts, pterygium and eye cancer, and that experts recommend lenses blocking at least 99 percent of UVA and UVB up to 400 nm, labeled UV400; the EU standard requires 95 percent up to 380 nm.[3] It also reports that dark lenses without UV protection can be worse than no sunglasses, because the pupil dilates and admits more UV, and that price is not a reliable sign of UV protection.[3] Yellow lenses are not recommended for night driving.[3]

A laboratory study of 20 young subjects compared clear lenses with yellow, dark yellow and orange lenses and linked the contrast enhancement of yellow lenses to selective reduction of short-wavelength light.[1] A later study reported that tinted lenses enhanced contrast sensitivity while causing losses of chromatic discrimination.[2] A literature review examined whether tinted lenses or filters improve visual performance in low vision.[6]

A 2021 study examined how blue-blocking lenses affect colour discrimination [7], and a small randomised crossover trial of 29 participants with visual stress found that a range of lens colours were beneficial, with precise colour matching not adding to the effect [8].

Photophobia, or light sensitivity, has many causes including migraine, cataracts, uveitis, corneal injury and some medications, and tinted glasses are sometimes used to manage it; precision tinted lenses are described as blocking the green-to-blue end of the spectrum without impairing vision.[9] People with light-sensitive conditions therefore wear colored lenses indoors as well as outdoors, which is a separate use from fashion tints.

FL-41 tinted lenses were tested in randomised crossover studies of benign essential blepharospasm, where they were compared with gray lenses for blink frequency and light sensitivity.[10] Tinted spectacles have also been studied in visually sensitive migraine.[11] Interventions that reduce evening blue-light exposure were reviewed in a meta-analysis for effects on sleep.[12]

Forum discussion of sunglasses on T Nation includes a self-described sunglass enthusiast listing several performance brands and a member describing a polarized pair that came with four interchangeable lenses in yellow, orange, clear and tinted, praised for athletic use.[13][14]
No studies found on coloured sunglasses and facial appearance. Studies of tinted lenses exist for contrast, light sensitivity and migraine, as described above.[1][2][10][11]

lore.intro: Discussion of tinted lenses mixes style opinion from retailers with optometry research on contrast and light sensitivity; forum talk on T Nation centres on performance eyewear [13][14][4].
